extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for improv games, warm-ups, scenework, and teaching a Level One improv syllabus; includes definitions of core improv concepts and practical tips for running exercises and public shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept
rubrics_metrics.description: Embracing an offer, the opposite of blocking. In Chicago, the term 'yield' is sometimes used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept other players' offers and build on them rather than denying reality; see Offer and Block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block (Deny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventing an action from continuing or denying the reality of an offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocking is often used by anxious improvisers to maintain control or to make audiences laugh, but it kills the story. (Chicago term: 'deny').

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new idea brought into an improvised scene, whether a line of dialogue, gesture, mime or whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and build on offers; offers can be lines, gestures, mimes—use them to grow the scene (see Accept, Block).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer which foretells another offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making promises and keeping them draws audiences in; use promises to establish expectations you later fulfil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reincorporation / Callback
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeding earlier elements back in to a story to give it structure. Referring to an element from earlier in the show (typically from another scene) as a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reincorporation adds structure and payoff; callbacks are a common form—plan to reuse earlier elements for cohesion and laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity Curve
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that a scene which gets progressively more absurd will hold the audience, whereas the absurd offer which comes at the end of that process would not be acceptable without that build-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build absurdity gradually; escalating absurdity is effective, sudden absurdity without a platform usually fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the Game
rubrics_metrics.description: See Game. The idea of identifying the pattern or 'game' in a scene which provides the scene's point of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeating patterns, promises, or mismatches in the scene and heighten them; finding the game gives a scene shape and comedic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game / Handle
rubrics_metrics.description: a) A formal structure imposed on a scene before it starts, also known as a Handle. b) Any pattern which occurs within a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games can help structure performance but can also ‘nail improvisers down’ and constrain imagination if overapplied; use games thoughtfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform
rubrics_metrics.description: The stable situation which exists at the beginning of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the platform before creating dramatic events; without a platform the audience can't understand stakes or cause-and-effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instant Trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: A way of killing stories by having dramatic events occur before the platform has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing high-stakes drama before the audience understands the situation; build platform first, then trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heighten / Raise the Stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: A Chicago term which roughly equates to raising the stakes or going up the absurdity curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heightening to make scenes more interesting; anxious improvisers often do the opposite—avoid lowering stakes merely to get a laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Total commitment to a role or game element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great energy, wit and daring can save almost any game; commit fully to choices (example: 'Never Touch The Floor Boy' saved by total commitment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenework (Open Scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of creating open scenes. A chunk of improvisation with no other handle or game to play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate open scenework from game-based scenes; practice building narrative, platform, and promises without a formal handle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Circle
rubrics_metrics.description: A way of thinking about the audience’s expectations. Given a particular set of story elements, some further elements seem very likely also to be included (inside the circle). Elements from outside the circle should not be included without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect audience expectations (inside-circle elements) unless you can justify breaking them; use the circle to judge what belongs in a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fog of War
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that improvisers are easily distracted by the stress of the situation and will fail to see or hear things that are easily noticed by the more relaxed audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exercises and direction to reduce stress and help players perceive obvious offers; be aware players may miss cues under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gag vs Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Gag: A laugh at the expense of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prioritizing gags that derail plot or promise—gags can be useful but should not undermine the scene's platform or narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joining
rubrics_metrics.description: Two improvisers adopting the same attitude or the same emotional state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use joining to create alignment and clarity between players; joining can strengthen scenes and make offers easier to accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify / Jump and Justify / Bridge
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sense of an offer, or put it in context after it has been made. Bridge: Taking your time to achieve an obvious end-point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use justification and bridging to connect offers to story logic; avoid apologizing for offers (Mick Napier's usage of 'justify' as negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment
rubrics_metrics.description: a) Adding a detail to someone else’s character or another element in the scene. b) A class of improv games in which one or more players has to guess secret information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer endowments to enrich scenes; use endowment games as exercises in specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise and Payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise is an offer that foretells another offer; keeping promises draws the audience in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish promises early and plan to deliver on them for satisfying payoffs and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory that an audience at an improv show is relating to not only the story the improvisers are telling (the First Story) but also the story of them telling it (the Second Story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware audiences follow both narratives—manage choices and visible process to enhance both stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of Obviousness (Obvious)
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer which could have been predicted by earlier offers. Generally a sign that things are going well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being 'obvious' can indicate good scene logic; don't fear predictable continuations if they follow naturally from the platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer which has no relation to earlier offers. Generally a sign that things are going badly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unrelated 'original' offers that break scene coherence unless intentionally justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sidetrack / That's Not Good Enough
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer which takes the story off in a new, uncalled-for direction. Unconscious strategy adopted by anxious improvisers of hopping from idea to idea instead of pushing one idea into the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for sidetracking and encourage players to push and deepen existing ideas rather than jumping to fresh, unrelated ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format (Competitive and Long vs Short Form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanism for packaging improvisation for public consumption, e.g., Theatresports. Long Form sustains over much of a show; Short Form consists of short discrete scenes or games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose format appropriate to performers and audience; competitive formats add elimination/scoring elements and change player behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-Coach / Directing
rubrics_metrics.description: Directing in a workshop: calling out instructions for students to follow while a scene is in progress. Direct/Director can also refer to live public direction during the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use side-coaching to shape learning; public directing changes the show dynamic—use sparingly and clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform / Exposition (avoid premature exposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stable situation which exists at the beginning of the story; exposition should establish platform without stalling momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance giving enough exposition to understand stakes with keeping pace; don't dump exposition that kills spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety / Physical Risk Guidance (Fling Shoo-ey)
rubrics_metrics.description: When playing physical games (e.g., shoe-tossing), ensure there is no risk provided people don’t hurl the shoes; remove enormous heavy hobnailed boots from play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk-assess games and adjust props/clothing to keep participants safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm-up Priority: Speed & Playfulness over Wit (I Am... game)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a great yes-and warm up, which also allows people to be funny if they want to. Prioritize speed and playfulness over wit, however, and be on your guard for people who come in third and ignore the second element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In warm-ups emphasize rapid responses and ensemble play rather than cleverness; monitor for anti-patterns like ignoring preceding offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate Struggling Players (Electric Company guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage people who struggle to come up with the 'right' word or a 'clever' word to just spit something out and to hit the rhythm. Their choice will be validated by the group repeating the two-word phrase anyway, even if it’s 'Roof-aargghh!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group repetition and rhythm to support lower-confidence players; normalize imperfect contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure Everyone Has a Turn (Spotlight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist that everybody has a turn, although if you play for long enough, even people who look aghast at the beginning will be singing along with everyone else, and taking their turn in the middle, too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure warm-ups and pre-show exercises to include all participants and build ensemble confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Response to Failure (More Stories Like That)
rubrics_metrics.description: If anyone stumbles, either over the template or the content, the whole group shouts 'Yay!' and three more people rush up to have a turn (this is part of the fun, so don’t give people too much time to memorize the sequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn mistakes into positive, fast-moving transitions to keep energy high and reduce performance anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes Let's / Nope (quality control dynamic)
rubrics_metrics.description: One person makes suggestions about how their story should continue; partner responds 'Yes let’s!' if they want it or 'Nope!' if not. Remind suggestion-makers that their partner is responsible for quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach performers that 'Nope!' can inspire better offers; encourage deliberate use of 'Nope' to improve scene quality. Variation: the 'Nope' player becomes suggestion-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: You (pattern-sustain & multi-pattern training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by establishing one pattern (pointing and saying 'You'), then repeat with categories (capital cities), then add a third physical pattern; the exercise builds to sustaining multiple patterns simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train responsibility: the sender must maintain patterns (if recipient misses it, sender politely continues); exercise calms panickers as panic doesn't make the task easier; use variations (e.g., intentionally mismatching names) to increase difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibbity Bibbity Bop (warm-up rules and variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: One player stands in middle of circle and uses strategies to get someone 'out'—e.g., point and say 'Bibbity bibbity bop' (target must say 'Bop' first) or point and just say 'Bop' (target must say nothing). Other variants involve a count to ten to arrange people into configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a rapid, playful warm-up, especially good with children; dozens of variations exist—try it to build alertness and group reflexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big Booty (group rhythmic game)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suitable for 5–10; one person 'Big Booty' numbers people and chants 'Big booty number x' in rhythm; number x must respond 'Number x, number y'. If someone screws up, group cries 'Oh shit!' and positions change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythm and sequencing to practice attention and timing; variations: replace numbers with words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fling Shoo-ey (physical coordination exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Players take off one shoe, toss gently across circle to someone with hand up, establishing a sequence; can add multiple shoes as skill increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep throws gentle; ensure shoes are safe to toss and remove hazardous footwear; progress by adding more shoes gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greetings (style variation exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have everyone march and introduce themselves and shake hands, then repeat in different styles (e.g., too enthusiastic, at a funeral, flirtatiously without touching, as bitter business rivals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use varied styles to practice character, status, and physicality; list of suggested styles provided to prompt choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotlight (singing-turn exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: One person sings a song in the middle; others who are reminded or if the singer falters, tag them and start a new song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great pre-show warm-up focused on bonding and fun; insist on inclusive participation and remove fear of 'getting it wrong.'

rubrics_metrics.name: I Am, I Am, I Am, I'll Take (tableau and removal exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: One person announces what they are and strikes a pose; others join to form a tableau. Then one element is removed and remaining player restates role and play continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong yes-and warm-up; prioritize speed and playfulness; guard against third entrants ignoring the second person's element.

rubrics_metrics.name: More Stories Like That (story-template exercise rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three improvisers tell a story using a repeating template of lines (Once upon a time..., And every day..., Until one day..., And because of that..., Until finally..., And ever since then...). If anyone stumbles, group shouts 'Yay!' and new players replace them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the template to teach narrative beats and rapid ensemble switching; keep turns short to discourage memorization and encourage spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings and Exits (Entrances and Exits guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Games that prescribe order of entrance/exit nail improvisers down rather than inspiring imagination; strict orders can constrain rather than free players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about using rigid entrance/exit structures—if they don't inspire imagination, consider freer variants; pre-planning names may work for some groups but can be limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: That’s Not Good Enough (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious strategy adopted by anxious improvisers of hopping from idea to idea instead of pushing one idea into the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coach players to push and deepen rather than abandon ideas; use exercises to practise sustaining a single idea to its natural heightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wimp / Wimping / Define (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to define; adding information weakly or not committing to specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage players to define elements clearly and not to rely on vague or half-hearted offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with Status
rubrics_metrics.description: Status (high/low) is a core tool and there are many status-based games and exercises (e.g., Low Status Clowns, Status Parties, Fight For Your Number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use status exercises to teach power dynamics, character choices and physicality; status can drive conflict and clarity in scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Interaction / Suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask For: A question you ask the audience to solicit an idea to inspire an improvised scene or game. Also, the answer to that question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience suggestions to seed scenes; craft asks that are specific enough to spark platform but open enough for creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination / Competitive Mechanics (when used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formats that include elimination or scoring (e.g., Theatresports, Micetro) change dynamics and can be used for extra audience interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that competitive formats alter player risk-taking and may require different directing and judging standards.
